tagline: A rural highway through wet savannas where insect-eating plants grow
intro: NC 211 is predominantly a two-lane rural highway, crossing the Green Swamp Preserve between Bolton and Supply. Wet longleaf pine savanna supports insect-eating plants in damp, nutrient-poor soil beneath an open understory. NCDOT includes Green Swamp in its scenic-byways guide, a program intended to introduce travelers to North Carolina’s history, geography and culture. The preserve’s wetlands have high water tables and long periods of saturated soil, conditions that support its varied plant communities.

The numbered highway began in 1921 with a route from Clarkton to Lumberton. It extended south to Bolton in 1930, then reached Supply in the mid-1950s. Later changes shifted traffic away from central Bladenboro: new alignments in 1972 and 1975 left the former town route as NC 211 Business. The business route through Bladenboro follows Martin Luther King Jr Drive and Seaboard Street, retaining the highway’s former passage through town.

Traveling toward the coast, the highway passes north of Bladenboro and through Clarkton before reaching Bolton. From Bolton, the swamp section runs almost due south toward Supply and US 17. Lake Waccamaw State Park lies along the shore of a Carolina bay; Crusoe Island is a separate community south of the lake beside the Waccamaw River.

moments.title: Lake Waccamaw
moments.text: Lake Waccamaw is a Carolina bay, with a state park occupying part of its shore. The U.S. Geological Survey interprets Carolina bays as remnants of thermokarst lakes formed thousands of years ago in a colder, drier and windier climate. In that explanation, frozen ground thawed to create lakes, which wind and water subsequently reshaped. The interpretation suggests that permafrost once reached this far south during the last ice age or earlier ice ages. The state park covers 2,398 acres near the town of Lake Waccamaw, within North Carolina’s Coastal Plain.

moments.title: Crusoe Island
moments.text: Crusoe Island is registered as Riverview and known locally as Crusoe. A few families make their homes in this unincorporated community in the Green Swamp. It borders the Waccamaw River just south of Lake Waccamaw, in Columbus County.

moments.title: Green Swamp Preserve
moments.text: The Green Swamp holds one of the largest wild populations of Venus flytraps, a plant native to a small area around Wilmington. Pitcher plants and sundews grow here too. The wet longleaf pine savanna supplies damp, nutrient-poor soil and an open understory. Researchers Walker and Peet reported that fire removes accumulated grasses and sedges and limits woody growth, maintaining conditions for smaller plants. The Nature Conservancy manages the preserve and plans fires to maintain these fire-dependent habitats. The swamp received National Natural Landmark designation in 1974, while the Nature Conservancy now manages more than 17,424 acres.
